hypothesis: HT-Breakout may have a repeatable route-side interaction: its HYPE long implementation may retain positive after-cost expectancy while the current short implementation and direct transfer to BTC, ETH, or SOL may require different context or exit treatment.
decision: Predeclare a route-and-side forward challenger using the existing bidirectional live telemetry. Keep long and short execution available on every authorized core asset; do not suppress shorts, restrict HT-Breakout to HYPE, change sizing, or alter exits from this small historical split. Attribute every future HT-Breakout lifecycle by exact coin, side, entry relation, fees, funding, slippage, MFE, MAE, exit reason, and net return on margin, then compare new forward results with the frozen baseline without pooling different route-side contracts.
falsifier: The HYPE-long hypothesis weakens if new independently resolved HYPE longs are net-negative after costs or if its profit factor falls below one. The transfer/short concern weakens if new BTC, ETH, SOL, or HYPE short cohorts become positive after costs with stable fill and protection evidence. Any missing route-side attribution or changed evidence hash invalidates the comparison.
limitations: The baseline has only 18 closes, and every non-HYPE asset has only two HT-Breakout trades.
HYPE long and short trades occurred at different times and possibly under different profiles and notionals; the comparison is not randomized.
BTC, ETH, and SOL have no closed HT-Breakout longs, so cross-asset long transfer is missing evidence rather than a failed result.
All-time compatible history is descriptive and cannot establish expected income, annualized return, or future profit factor.
Existing route-side telemetry is sufficient for prospective measurement; no new model, filter, gate, or strategy mutation is authorized by this record.
